User: That sounds great! Can you give me instructions on making salt dough ornaments?
Assistant: Of course! Here is a simple recipe for making salt dough ornaments:

Ingredients:
- 2 cups all-purpose flour
- 1 cup salt
- 1 cup warm water
- food coloring (optional)
- rolling pin
- cookie cutters
- straw
- baking sheet
- ribbon or string

Instructions:

1. In a large mixing bowl, combine the flour, salt, and warm water. Mix until dough forms. If you want colored ornaments, you can add food coloring to the dough now and knead it until the color is evenly distributed.

2. Roll out the dough on a floured surface until it’s about 1/4 inch thick.

3. Use cookie cutters to cut out different shapes for your ornaments.

4. Using a straw or toothpick, make a small hole at the top of each ornament for the ribbon or string to hang from.

5. Preheat your oven to 250°F (120°C). Place your ornaments on a baking sheet lined with parchment paper.

6. Bake the ornaments for about 2 hours or until they’re completely dry and hard to the touch.

7. Let the ornaments cool completely before decorating them with paint, markers, or glitter.

8. Once decorated, string a ribbon or string through the hole you made earlier and tie it in a knot.

Your salt dough ornaments are now ready to hang on your Christmas tree or give as gifts to family and friends.
User: That's awesome! Can you also suggest some ideas for decorating salt dough ornaments?
Assistant: Certainly! Here are a few ideas for decorating your salt dough ornaments:

1. Paint: Once the ornaments have cooled completely, you can use acrylic paint to add details and designs. You can also add a layer of clear sealant to protect the paint.

2. Glitter: Add a touch of sparkle to your ornaments by covering them with glue and sprinkling glitter over them. You can use one color of glitter or multiple colors for a fun, festive look.

3. Marker: If you prefer a simpler look, you can use markers to draw designs onto the ornaments. This is a great option for younger children who may have a harder time with more intricate designs.

4. Beads: You can glue small beads onto your ornaments to add texture and visual interest. This is a great way to create patterns or images.

5. Personalization: Use a fine-tipped marker or paint to add names, dates, or messages to your ornaments. This is a great way to make the ornaments more special and personalized.

6. Mod Podge: Use Mod Podge or another clear sealant to apply paper or fabric to your ornaments. This is a great way to create a unique look and use up any scraps of paper or fabric you have lying around.

Remember, the possibilities are endless when it comes to decorating your salt dough ornaments. Get creative and have fun with it!
User: How did the author afford to travel during their study abroad semester?: Most weekends this semester, you’d find me in or around St Andrews, Scotland. Unlike many study abroad students, I have not been doing as much traveling this semester.
Don’t get me wrong: I love traveling and I think it’s a great part of your study abroad experience. Due in part to my limited finances, however, I usually spend my time much closer to school.
Last semester, I also saved most of my money from my work-study job on campus for travel and spending money. This bolstered my bank account for the inevitable costs of international travel and living in a country with a strong currency like the British pound.
Most of this money, however, I was saving for a trip in continental Europe, when I visited France, Germany, and the Netherlands by train. I had never been to these countries before and knew studying so nearby was a chance I could not pass up!
Since I am used to having a job during the school year, I looked for ways I might be able to sustaining an income while abroad. Researching my short-term student visa, I found it would not allow me to work while in the UK. Then I discovered IFSA-Butler’s work-to-study program, and I was lucky enough to get one of the positions on offer. This has helped to maintain my living money as well.
With enough financial planning and forethought, it is possible even for students heavily reliant on financial aid like myself to travel while abroad!
Despite my main trip over spring break and another weekend trip or two, however, I’m usually not far from St Andrews. And to be honest, I’m quite happy with this.
It can be hard, of course, to see other students traveling throughout the semester—that sinking feeling that perhaps you aren’t “making the most of it.” But I have grown to really appreciate what this little seaside Scottish town has to offer, and it’s begun to feel like home in just a few short months.
When I first decided to study in Scotland, it was a bit of a promised land in my mind—a new and fresh start for the semester. Then as I boarded the plane for my transatlantic flight, fears of how it couldn’t possibly live up to these high expectations flashed through my mind. Yet, since arriving here it really has. I have loved settling into my new home and treating it like just that: a new home.
Rather than using it as a base from which to explore other parts of Europe, I have enjoyed engaging more with the area itself. It’s the little things—such as a longer chat with the cashier at the grocery store about how one of her kids went to St Andrews, finding hidden park trails for relaxing walks, or having a usual order at a local pub—that really make you feel at home.
Bonding with other students usually happens rather organically, but interacting with the locals can require a bit more effort on a university student’s part. But that extra effort pays off, as you really get to know the culture of the area more, not just the university’s culture.
Plus, this part of Scotland is so beautiful that walks around town and through the countryside feel as fulfilling as a day full of traveling. User: That sounds great! Can you give me instructions on making salt dough ornaments?
Assistant: Of course! Here is a simple recipe for making salt dough ornaments:

Ingredients:
- 2 cups all-purpose flour
- 1 cup salt
- 1 cup warm water
- food coloring (optional)
- rolling pin
- cookie cutters
- straw
- baking sheet
- ribbon or string

Instructions:

1. In a large mixing bowl, combine the flour, salt, and warm water. Mix until dough forms. If you want colored ornaments, you can add food coloring to the dough now and knead it until the color is evenly distributed.

2. Roll out the dough on a floured surface until it’s about 1/4 inch thick.

3. Use cookie cutters to cut out different shapes for your ornaments.

4. Using a straw or toothpick, make a small hole at the top of each ornament for the ribbon or string to hang from.

5. Preheat your oven to 250°F (120°C). Place your ornaments on a baking sheet lined with parchment paper.

6. Bake the ornaments for about 2 hours or until they’re completely dry and hard to the touch.

7. Let the ornaments cool completely before decorating them with paint, markers, or glitter.

8. Once decorated, string a ribbon or string through the hole you made earlier and tie it in a knot.

Your salt dough ornaments are now ready to hang on your Christmas tree or give as gifts to family and friends.

- straw
- baking sheet
- ribbon or string

7. Let the ornaments cool completely before decorating them with paint, markers, or glitter.

8. Once decorated, string a ribbon or string through the hole you made earlier and tie it in a knot.

Your salt dough ornaments are now ready to hang on your Christmas tree or give as gifts to family and friends.

Use a clear, engaging speaking style that connects with your audience and highlights the importance of financial preparedness. Be sure to anticipate and address any potential counterarguments or objections to your position.
Assistant: Good evening, ladies and gentlemen,

Tonight, I want to talk to you about something that is often overlooked but is critical for everyone's financial well-being: emergency funds. As we all know, life is full of surprises, and money is often at the center of these surprises. From unexpected job loss to medical emergencies, we have all faced situations where we needed money urgently but had none at hand. This is where emergency funds come in handy.

An emergency fund is a set amount of money that you have saved for unexpected expenses. It is different from your regular savings account as it is earmarked specifically for emergencies. Having one can mean the difference between financial ruin and weathering a storm. 

So why is an emergency fund crucial? Firstly, it provides a safety net in the event of an unexpected expense. Let's say you break your leg and need immediate medical attention. If you have an emergency fund, you can use it to cover the expenses without worrying about how you will pay for them. Without an emergency fund, you may be forced to borrow money or rely on credit, which can lead to debt and financial ruin.

Secondly, it provides a sense of security and peace of mind. Knowing that you have a cushion to fall back on in times of crisis can alleviate a lot of financial stress. This, in turn, can help you focus on other areas of your life, such as your health, job, or family.

Now, you may be thinking, "I don't have enough money to save for an emergency fund." But that is simply not true. Building an emergency fund does not have to happen overnight. You can start small, even if it means saving just $5 a week. Over time, these small amounts add up and can make a significant difference. Another way to build an emergency fund is to set up an automatic transfer from your checking account to your emergency fund every month. This way, you won't even notice the money is gone until you need it.

In addition to saving, there are other strategies that can help you build and maintain an emergency fund. For example, consider cutting back on unnecessary expenses, such as eating out or buying clothes you don't need. Use coupons and take advantage of sales to stretch your dollar. Also, consider setting up a side hustle or taking on freelance work to earn extra income that you can dedicate to your emergency fund.

In conclusion, emergencies are inevitable, but financial ruin is not. Building an emergency fund is crucial for everyone's financial well-being. It may take some time and sacrifice, but the peace of mind and financial security it provides is worth it. So, start saving today and make sure that you have the security and peace of mind that comes with having an emergency fund. Thank you.

c67-m1.summary: The user is a retired librarian.
c67-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Hi, I'm looking for some music recommendations. I've been feeling a bit stuck in my current playlist.
Assistant: I'd be happy to help! Can you tell me a bit more about the kind of music you're into? What genres or artists do you usually listen to?
User: I'm pretty open to anything, but I tend to lean towards punk and new wave. I love the energy and the rebellious spirit of those genres.
Assistant: Great taste! Punk and new wave are amazing genres. Have you listened to any of the classic German post-punk bands like Kraftwerk or Neu!?
User: Actually, I'm not super familiar with the German post-punk scene, but I do love some of the more avant-garde and experimental artists from that era.
Assistant: Well, you might enjoy some of the more eccentric artists from that time period. There was a lot of experimentation and pushing of boundaries going on in the German music scene in the 70s and 80s.
User: Yeah, that sounds really interesting. I love when artists push the boundaries of what's considered "normal" in music.
Assistant: Absolutely! One artist who comes to mind is Nina Hagen. She was a German singer who was known for her outrageous and unconventional style, both musically and visually.
User: (laughs) Actually, I've met someone recently who is a huge fan of Nina Hagen. I've been meaning to check out her music more.
Assistant: No way! That's a great coincidence. Nina Hagen is definitely a cult figure, and her fans are very devoted. What's this person like who's a fan of hers?
User: Well, they're definitely... enthusiastic. They have all of her albums on vinyl and can recite all of the lyrics by heart. It's pretty impressive, actually.
Assistant: (laughs) That sounds like a true superfan! It's great when people are so passionate about an artist's music. Has this person introduced you to any of Nina Hagen's songs or albums that you particularly enjoy?
User: Yeah, they've been playing her album "Nun Sex Monk Rock" nonstop, and I have to say, it's definitely grown on me. The way she blends punk and reggae influences is really interesting.
Assistant: That's a great album! "Nun Sex Monk Rock" is definitely one of Nina Hagen's most iconic works. It's amazing how well it holds up even today.
User: Totally. And it's been great to see how much joy it brings this person. They're always singing along and dancing to the music. It's infectious!
Assistant: That's the best part of being a fan, isn't it? When the music brings you so much happiness and energy. It's great that you're getting to experience that through this person's love of Nina Hagen's music.
User: Hi, I'm feeling a bit overwhelmed lately. I'm not sure how to manage my time effectively.
Assistant: I'd be happy to help you with that. Can you tell me a bit more about what's been going on and how you've been spending your time?
User: Well, I just feel like I have too many things on my plate. I'm having trouble focusing on one thing at a time.
Assistant: It sounds like you might be feeling a bit scattered. Have you tried making a to-do list or setting priorities for yourself?
User: Yeah, I've tried that. But it's not just about getting things done. I feel like I need to be able to focus on something for a longer period of time.
Assistant: I understand what you mean. Being able to focus for an extended period of time can be really beneficial for productivity and learning. Is there something specific that you're trying to accomplish or learn?
User: Yeah... actually, I've recently started learning a new skill. It's been a bit of a challenge for me.
Assistant: Learning a new skill can be both exciting and intimidating. What kind of skill are you trying to learn?
User: It's a musical instrument. I've always wanted to play, but it's harder than I thought it would be.
Assistant: That's great that you're taking the initiative to learn something new! Playing a musical instrument requires a lot of dedication and practice. What's been the most challenging part for you so far?
User: I think it's just the amount of time and effort required to see progress. I feel like I need to practice every day, but it's hard to fit it into my schedule.
Assistant: Consistency is key when it comes to learning a new skill, especially one that requires physical practice like playing an instrument. Have you tried setting aside a specific time each day to practice?
User: Yeah, I've been trying to do that. But it's not just about finding the time. It's also about being able to focus during that time. I find my mind wandering a lot when I'm practicing.
Assistant: It's normal for your mind to wander, especially when you're doing something new and challenging. One strategy that might help is to set specific goals for each practice session. This can help you stay focused and motivated.
User: That's a great idea. I think I'll try that. Thanks for the advice!
Assistant: You're welcome! Remember that learning a new skill takes time and effort, but it's worth it in the end. Don't be too hard on yourself if you don't see progress right away. Just keep practicing and you'll get there eventually.

User: Hey, I've been listening to a lot of music lately and I'm looking for some new artists to check out. Do you have any recommendations?
Assistant: Ah, that's great! I'd be happy to help you discover some new music. What kind of genres or styles are you into? Are you looking for something mellow or something more upbeat?
User: I'm pretty open to anything, but I've been listening to a lot of 80s and 90s music lately. I love the energy and the creativity of that era.
Assistant: That's a great era for music! There were so many iconic artists and bands that came out during that time. Have you listened to any German music from that era? They had a pretty vibrant scene back then.
User: Actually, I haven't listened to much German music. But I do know of a few artists like Nena and Alphaville. What else would you recommend?
Assistant: Those are great starting points! Another artist you might want to check out is Nina Hagen. She's a German singer-songwriter who was really popular in the 80s and 90s. She's known for her unique voice and style, which blends elements of punk, new wave, and pop.
User: Oh, I've heard of her! I've listened to a few of her songs, but I don't know much about her music beyond that. What would you recommend as a good starting point?
Assistant: Well, if you want to get a feel for her style, I'd recommend checking out some of her most popular songs like "99 Luftballons" or "Universal Radio". But if you want to dig deeper, she has a really diverse discography that's worth exploring.
User: Yeah, I think I'd like to explore her music a bit more. I've been trying to get into the habit of listening to more than just an artist's greatest hits. I feel like there's often so much more to their music than what's on the surface.
Assistant: Absolutely! I think that's a great approach to music listening. When you only listen to an artist's most popular songs, you can miss out on some really great hidden gems. Do you have a strategy for discovering those lesser-known tracks, or is it more of a random process for you?
User: Well, actually, I make it a point to listen to Nina Hagen's lesser-known tracks to deepen my appreciation for her music. I figure that if I only listen to her most popular songs, I'm not really getting a complete picture of who she is as an artist.
Assistant: That's a great approach! By listening to her lesser-known tracks, you're not only getting a more well-rounded understanding of her music, but you're also showing respect for her as an artist. It's like you're saying, "I value your entire body of work, not just the stuff that's most popular."
User: Exactly! And I feel like it's also a way of paying homage to her creativity and experimentation. I mean, she's an artist who's not afraid to take risks and try new things, and that's something that I really admire.
Assistant: Absolutely. Nina Hagen is definitely an artist who has never been afraid to push boundaries and challenge her listeners. And I think that's part of what makes her music so enduring – it's not just catchy and fun, but it's also thought-provoking and emotionally resonant.
User: Yeah, I can see that. Even in her lesser-known tracks, there's a level of depth and complexity that's really impressive. Do you have any favorite Nina Hagen songs or albums that might be considered lesser-known?
Assistant: Actually, I think one of her most underrated albums is "Freudiana". It's a concept album that explores the ideas of Sigmund Freud, and it's just incredibly clever and musically diverse. It's not as well-known as some of her other work, but it's definitely worth checking out if you're looking to dig deeper into her discography.
User: Hey, what kind of music do you think is making a comeback lately?
Assistant: Ah, that's an interesting question. I've seen a resurgence of 80s-inspired genres like synth-pop and new wave. Even some punk influences are sneaking their way back into modern music. What about you, do you have a favorite music genre?

Assistant: Live music is the best, isn't it? There's nothing quite like the rush of adrenaline you get from watching your favorite artists perform live. Have you been to any exciting concerts or festivals recently?
User: Not too many, but I'm planning to change that soon. I want to attend more music events and discover new artists. Do you think festivals are a good way to find new music?
Assistant: Festivals are an amazing way to discover new artists and genres. You get to experience a variety of acts in one place, and sometimes you stumble upon someone you've never heard of before, and they end up becoming your new favorite artist. What kind of festivals are you thinking of attending?

Assistant: Yeah, Coachella is definitely a popular one, but sometimes the smaller festivals can be more fun and intimate. If you're looking for something specific, like punk or new wave, you might want to check out some of the smaller festivals that cater to those genres.
User: That's a great idea. I've recently started attending music festivals that feature punk and new wave artists, hoping to discover new favorites. The last one I went to was a lot of fun, but I felt a bit overwhelmed by the number of bands playing at the same time. Do you have any tips on how to navigate a festival schedule?
Assistant: Ah, I'm glad you're having fun! Navigating a festival schedule can be tough, but I've got a few tips that might help. First, make a list of your must-see bands and prioritize those. Then, take a look at the schedule and plan out your day, including some buffer time in case you want to check out some new artists or grab some food. You can also consider using the festival app to stay up-to-date on the schedule and any last-minute changes.
User: That's really helpful, thanks! I also noticed that some of the bands I wanted to see were playing at the same time, which was frustrating. Is there a way to avoid those conflicts?
Assistant: Yeah, conflicts can be tough! One strategy is to identify the bands you really want to see and then look for other bands that are playing at different times. You can also consider splitting your time between two stages if the bands are playing at the same time. It's not ideal, but it's better than missing out on someone you really want to see.
User: Okay, I think I have a better plan now. What about discovering new artists? Are there any tips for finding the hidden gems at a festival?
Assistant: Ah, discovering new artists is one of the best parts of a festival! I'd recommend checking out the smaller stages or the early afternoon slots, where you might find some up-and-coming bands. You can also ask other festival-goers for recommendations or check out the festival's social media accounts to see who they're highlighting as must-see acts.
User: That's a great idea. I'll definitely do some research beforehand and ask around during the festival. Thanks for all the tips – I feel way more prepared now!
Assistant: You're welcome! I'm glad I could help. Have a blast at the festival, and I hope you discover some amazing new artists!

c101-m1.summary: Nina Simone's music was deeply influenced by her experiences as a Black woman in the American South, reflecting her struggles with racial injustice and personal heartbreak.
c101-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Breaking her foot mid-song at the Coachella Valley Music & Arts Festival in Indio in April was a painful but unexpectedly eye-opening experience for Florence Welch.
Happily, she has recovered from her onstage Coachella mishap and is sitting no more.
Now on tour in support of her fourth and most emotionally revealing album, the chart-topping “How Big, How Blue, How Beautiful,” she and her band, The Machine, perform Wednesday at SDSU’s Viejas Arena.
Welch, 29, spoke with the Union-Tribune by phone from England about her proudly offbeat, baroque style of pop, getting older and quitting drinking. Here are excerpts from that conversation. To read the full interview, go to sandiegouniontribune.com.
Q: Have you done more interviews in the past few years than you might ever care to recall?
A: I’ve done quite a few. It’s funny, because I don’t think musicians express themselves that well in conversation. We just write songs to best describe how we’re feeling.
Q: I’d like to ask some questions you might not normally be asked. To begin, you go up to that great nightclub in the sky. Sitting at three tables are Billie Holiday, Etta James and Nina Simone. You can only sit down and talk with one of them. Who do you pick, and why?
A: I think I’d like to go sit next to Billie. I’ve always been so fascinated by her and her voice. When I first became interested in music, the emotion and sadness behind her voice was always so captivating. I listened to it so much and was so drawn to it, and to her life and that whole era of music, of jazz.
Q: Has it become more important for you to use your music to tell the truth about your life, as you do on your new album?
A: I think very much so, yeah. And, as I get older, something in you (evolves). That holds especially true with this record. I don’t know what (specific) drive in me came into play with it. I think I tried to write about my life on my previous albums. But, because of fear, I would hide behind metaphors and disappear behind fantasy, which was wonderful to use my imagination. But getting older meant the songs became much more direct and literal. And that was quite important to me, as an artist, to feel that was OK and to kind of own it and own who I was. It was almost like I had to own the bad and the good, equally, to kind of be more vulnerable.
A: Hmm. I think it makes you - it’s just a rite of passage, isn’t it? You enter into the world of everyone else who’s had their heart broken. It just gives you another level of understanding of the human condition. You can be more empathetic. But ... Although it’s happened so many times to countless people, when it happens to you, it’s like you have to write songs about it. ... The only thing you can do when it happens to you is try to make something of it. It’s very humbling.
A: I don’t know. It’s all just experience. I think life, and really engaging in life, makes you a better songwriter. But, sometimes, I think being a musician is a perfect way not to engage in life, and (lets) you detach and live in a fantasy world.
A: That’s it! Sometimes, as a musician, the rate at which you grow is very much in your own hands, because you (can) stay like a child, forever. As long as you can go (perform a) show, the rest of your life can be total chaos. For me, having time alone and being responsible for myself when I was making this album showed me (what had been) my own self-destructive behavior.
Q: How scary was it for you to remove some of the protective musical and emotional layers with your new album?
A: It was frightening to release it because I felt very close to it. It’s almost like (while) it helped me to make it, “Do I have to tell people I feel better now?” But something happens in the alchemy of a live performance. When you sing it to an audience and they sing it back, it’s not yours anymore; it’s a shared experience.
Q: Prior to making “How Big,” you said you’d had a kind of “nervous breakdown” connected to your “on-off relationship” with drinking. Was there a tipping point for you?
A: I think the way that I grew up, going to parties and seeing punk bands play ... I grew up in very much of an art college, drinking culture, where - to perform - you’d grab a bottle of vodka and a can of paint, and get onstage and see what happens. I thought the amount you drank would determine how good the gig was, and that’s what I did, for years. It was this free-for-all, chaotic thing. And I don’t regret it, because that’s what it was.

Q: I’d like to ask some questions you might not normally be asked. To begin, you go up to that great nightclub in the sky. Sitting at three tables are Billie Holiday, Etta James and Nina Simone. You can only sit down and talk with one of them. Who do you pick, and why?
A: I think I’d like to go sit next to Billie. I’ve always been so fascinated by her and her voice. When I first became interested in music, the emotion and sadness behind her voice was always so captivating. I listened to it so much and was so drawn to it, and to her life and that whole era of music, of jazz.

I think I tried to write about my life on my previous albums. But, because of fear, I would hide behind metaphors and disappear behind fantasy, which was wonderful to use my imagination. But getting older meant the songs became much more direct and literal. And that was quite important to me, as an artist, to feel that was OK and to kind of own it and own who I was. It was almost like I had to own the bad and the good, equally, to kind of be more vulnerable.
A: Hmm. I think it makes you - it’s just a rite of passage, isn’t it? You enter into the world of everyone else who’s had their heart broken. It just gives you another level of understanding of the human condition. You can be more empathetic. But ... c103-m1.summary: The New York Times calls soprano Julia Bullock “an exceptional singer of the new generation.”
c103-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Here is a piece of text: When: Oct 21, 3 p.m.
The New York Times calls soprano Julia Bullock “an exceptional singer of the new generation.” She makes her Vancouver debut Oct. 21, with pianist John Arida, in a Vancouver Recital Society program of Schubert, Fauré, and various American composers.
Bullock, who hails from St. Louis, won first prize at the Young Concert Artists International Auditions in 2012 and then did the same at the 2014 Naumburg International Vocal Competition. And she has sung in opera and recitals ever since.
At 17 a family member gave Bullock a recording of famous classical female singers.
Managing her career has been a challenge for the fast-rising soprano.
Bullock currently divides her focus between the recital platform and the opera stage.
“I’m very happy with both. My introduction was through song, and in (recital) the relationship between the music and the lyrics can be so much more complicated than in opera, where you are contributing to a whole. But the demands are exactly the same — you need to be focused on a direct delivery of the text.
For her Vancouver appearance Bullock will sing music penned by American women, including Alberta Hunter, Lovie Austin, Billie Holiday, and Nina Simone. It’s no crossover stunt, but an exploration of tradition and identity.
Bullock’s Vancouver date is part of a six-city fall tour. She’s got another big project on tap this season as artist-in-residence at the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
And after they heard Bullock sing, a Met official made an offer.
Bullock’s Met adventure began last month with History’s Persistent Voice, a recital featuring traditional black slave songs and texts. In December she presents musical settings of words by Langston Hughes and a chamber version of John Adams’s nativity oratorio El Niño, before rounding out her residency in the new year with Tyshawn Sorey’s Perle Noire (Meditations for Joséphine) and a rare revival of Hans Werner Henze’s El Cimarrón.
Lucky New Yorkers. But lucky Vancouver to get an afternoon with Julia.
